## Research question & study area {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
Peatland fires in Central Kalimantan cause haze, health and economic harm. This study asks two questions of the 2026 satellite record:

-   **Q1** — Where does fire-detection intensity concentrate, and when?
-   **Q2** — Are detections significantly clustered, beyond just being dense?

Study window: **Kabupaten Pulang Pisau**, a peat-dominated regency — chosen because it is an administrative unit and dominated by fire-prone peatland.
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/plot-boundary-1.png)

::: caption
The regency boundary, used as the observation window for every analysis.
:::
::::
::::::

## Data & study design {.smaller}

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **Detections** | NASA FIRMS VIIRS 375 m (NOAA-20), 1 Jan – 23 Sep 2026 |
| **Boundary** | GADM ADM2 (regency), UTM 49S (EPSG:32749) |
| **Point event** | one detection ≠ one fire → de-duplicated to one point per pixel per day |
| **Cleaning** | 370,354 → 351,822 national → **16,189** inside the regency |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A detection is not a distinct fire — a fire burning over several days is picked up on several satellite overpasses, which inflates apparent clustering. De-duplication therefore comes first.
:::

## Analytical approach {.smaller}

The two questions are answered separately, because **intensity** (how many events, and where) and **interaction** (whether events cluster beyond that) are different properties. Following r4gdsa Ch. 4–6:

| Question            | Method                          | Compared against   |
|---------------------|---------------------------------|--------------------|
| Is it random?       | **Clark-Evans test**            | CSR (Monte Carlo)  |
| Where is intensity? | **Kernel density (KDE)**        | —                  |
| Do points interact? | **G / F / K / L functions**     | homogeneous CSR    |
| Robustness          | **Inhomogeneous L**             | inhomogeneous null |
| Timing              | **Spatio-temporal KDE** (sparr) | —                  |

## First-order — intensity concentrates in the south {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/kde-tmap-1.png)
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
*The map is a kernel density surface — darker/redder means more detections per km².*

**Clark-Evans R = 0.42** (p = 0.01): R below 1 means the points are **clustered, not random**.

The KDE hotspot sits in the **central-south peatland**, and stays there across all three bandwidths — so the peak is real, not an artefact of the smoothing choice. This matches the low-lying, fire-prone peat in that part of the regency.
:::
:::::

## Second-order — strong clustering vs CSR {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/lest-1.png)
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
*How to read it: the x-axis is distance; the grey band is what a random (CSR) pattern would look like. The observed curve (black) above the band means clustering at that distance.*

Here the observed **L-curve sits far above** the band across all scales up to \~20 km. G, F, K and L all agree — the detections are **significantly more clustered** than random, the signature of fires concentrated in a few active areas.
:::
:::::

## Value-added 1 — is the clustering real? {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/linhom-1.png)
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
The CSR test above assumes intensity is the *same everywhere*, which is false. The **inhomogeneous L** allows intensity to vary and re-tests.

*Reading it the same way: once intensity is allowed to vary, the curve now sits close to the baseline instead of far above it.*

**Key result:** the clustering mostly reflects **first-order heterogeneity** — fires concentrate because the *conditions* for fire concentrate — not extra fire-to-fire interaction.
:::
:::::

## Value-added 2 — activity builds up in time {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/stkde-plot-1.png)
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
*Each panel is the fire-density surface for one month (Jun–Sep); brighter means more intense activity that month.*

The spatio-temporal KDE shows the hotspot **stays in the central-south peatland** but **grows stronger** as the dry season advances.

So **timing matters as much as location** — the same core is at risk throughout, but the risk window concentrates in a few months.
:::
:::::

## Key findings {.smaller}

-   **First-order.** The Clark-Evans test (R = 0.42) confirms the detections are clustered rather than random, and the KDE shows this concentration sits firmly in the central-south peatland.
-   **Second-order.** All four distance functions (G, F, K, L) place the observed pattern well outside the CSR envelope, so the clustering is statistically significant, not just visible on a map.
-   **But the source of that clustering matters.** Once the inhomogeneous L allows intensity to vary, the signal largely disappears — meaning the clustering is driven by the uneven peatland, not by fires triggering one another.
-   **Timing.** The monthly spatio-temporal KDE shows activity is not constant through the year; it builds up and peaks during the dry-season months.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
First- and second-order evidence point the same way: a few peat-dominated areas drive the whole pattern. In practical terms, *where* the peat is matters far more than any interaction between individual fires — which is what makes targeted, location-based management sensible.
:::

## Limitations & implications {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Read with care**

-   Detections ≠ fires; cloud/overpass gaps.
-   Concentration ≠ risk without exposure data.
-   CSR/KDE assumptions only partly hold.
-   Window stops in September.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**From evidence to action**

-   **Where** — focus monitoring & patrols on the central-south peatland.
-   **When** — raise readiness ahead of the dry-season peak.
-   **Longer term** — peatland water management (levels, canal blocking).
:::
:::::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Directly supported by the analysis: **spatial concentration + timing**. Needs more data before acting: causation, and who/what is exposed.
:::
